text: Imagine you are traveling from London to Paris, then to New York.
Every time you land, what’s the very first thing you do?
Resetting your watch, of course.
But have you ever wondered why the whole world agreed to take Greenwich
— a small, quiet town on the outskirts of London — as the starting point zero for all time zones?
Why not glamorous Paris, modern Washington, or a neutral spot in the middle of the ocean?
The answer takes us back to the 19th century.
At that time, the concept of standard time didn’t exist at all.
Every city and town set its own local time based on the sun's position.
When the sun was directly overhead, that was 12 noon.
As a result, the United States had hundreds of different time zones,
and train travel in Britain was a chronological nightmare.
To solve this chaos, in October 1884,
the International Meridian Conference was held in Washington D.C.
Representatives from 25 nations debated fiercely to choose a single prime meridian.
The French, led by astronomer Jules Janssen, vehemently opposed choosing Greenwich.
They argued that the prime meridian had to be a completely neutral line,
not belonging to any global power.
They proposed placing it in the Azores or the Bering Strait,
just like how the metric system was created based on the size of the Earth, rather than a national landmark.
But the British and the Americans had a much more pragmatic argument:
72% of the world's shipping commerce at the time was already using charts based on the Greenwich meridian.
Starting over from scratch with a new location would cause a massive economic loss.
Finally, the vote took place.
22 countries voted in favor of Greenwich.
Only a single country voted against: San Domingo, now the Dominican Republic.
Two countries abstained: Brazil and, of course, France.
France refused to accept this defeat for decades.
They continued to use Paris time until 1911.
Even when they conceded, French law called the new time 'Paris mean time, retarded by 9 minutes and 21 seconds'
rather than ever calling it Greenwich time.
Today, the Greenwich Meridian is not just a metal strip on the ground at the Royal Observatory.
It is proof that sometimes, practical convenience and economic power shape how we measure the world,
rising above all political disputes.
